lead: The ultimate load method, also called ultimate load design or the load factor method, designs a reinforced concrete section to resist factored ultimate loads at collapse. It multiplies service loads by one global load factor, analyses the member for those ultimate loads, and checks that the section's ultimate strength is at least the required ultimate moment. Engineers used it as a step beyond working stress design because concrete and steel behave inelastically near failure. Current Indian practice uses limit state design, but the ultimate load method explains the collapse side of that idea clearly.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for service loads and permissible stresses, and Chapter 1.1 for the stress–strain limits behind ultimate strength.

sections.h3: The idea of a global load factor

blocks.text: The working stress method in Chapter 1.2 checks whether stresses at service loads stay below permissible values. The ultimate load method asks a different question: will the member stand when the loads reach their factored ultimate value? Service loads are the loads expected in normal use. Dead load comes from the member itself and the finishes; live load comes from people, furniture or stored goods. The global load factor γf is one number applied to the total service load. It lumps together load variation, material strength, construction quality and the consequence of failure. The method is also called ultimate load design or the load factor method.

blocks.where: w<sub>u</sub> is the ultimate load per metre, γ<sub>f</sub> is the global load factor, w<sub>D</sub> is the service dead load per metre and w<sub>L</sub> is the service live load per metre.

blocks.text: The required ultimate moment is found by analysing the member under w<sub>u</sub>. For a linear elastic analysis, M<sub>u,req</sub> = γ<sub>f</sub> M<sub>service</sub>. M<sub>service</sub> is the bending moment from unfactored service loads. The result is one design load and one design moment. There is no separate factor for dead load, live load, concrete or steel. That simplicity is the method's attraction and its weakness.

Ultimate strength is the load-carrying capacity just before failure. The collapse moment M<sub>u</sub> is the bending moment a section can carry at that stage. It is calculated from the ultimate strength of the materials: the concrete strength is taken as the cube strength f<sub>ck</sub> through an ultimate stress block whose maximum stress is a fraction of f<sub>ck</sub>, and steel at its yield strength f<sub>y</sub>; no material safety factor is applied to either. The section is then checked as M<sub>u</sub> ≥ M<sub>u,req</sub>. M<sub>u</sub> is the available collapse resistance; M<sub>u,req</sub> is the moment from factored ultimate loads.

The check covers collapse only. It does not directly check service deflection, crack width or durability. A beam may pass M<sub>u</sub> ≥ M<sub>u,req</sub> and still sag too much or crack visibly under normal service loads. It also gives no separate measure of ductility. If the section is over-reinforced, collapse can be sudden and brittle.

items: Advantage: it targets the real failure condition instead of an elastic stress limit.
Advantage: it uses the inelastic strength of concrete and steel, so it can be less conservative than working stress design.
Advantage: one global factor and one check make hand calculations short.
Limitation: service deflection and cracking are not checked.
Limitation: one factor cannot separate the variability of dead load, live load, concrete and steel.
Limitation: brittle failure remains a risk unless detailing and steel limits are enforced.

sections.h3: Why limit state design replaced it

blocks.text: Working stress design came first. Ultimate load design followed as engineers recognised that concrete and steel do not fail at elastic stress limits. Limit state design later kept the collapse check but added serviceability checks. It also replaced the single global factor with partial safety factors. Dead and live loads get different factors because their variability differs. Concrete and steel get separate material factors. This gives the designer control over each uncertainty.

The ultimate load method therefore survives as a teaching idea and as the collapse half of limit state design. It is not the current method for ordinary reinforced concrete design in Indian practice; Chapter 1.4 sets out the two-limit-state approach. Chapter 1.6 shows how characteristic values become design values. Use the ultimate load method to understand ultimate load, ultimate strength and the collapse check. Do not use it as a complete design method for a real beam.

figure.caption: Service loads are multiplied by a global load factor of 1.5 to obtain ultimate loads; the section is then checked so its collapse resistance is at least the required ultimate moment.

spec.title: Ultimate load method
spec.aria: A vertical flow multiplies service loads by a global load factor of 1.5 to obtain ultimate loads, then checks the section's collapse resistance against the required ultimate moment.

examples.question: A simply supported reinforced concrete beam spans 6.0 m and carries a service dead load of 12 kN/m and a service live load of 8 kN/m. Use a global load factor of 1.5. Find the required ultimate moment M<sub>u,req</sub>.
steps: Total service load w = w<sub>D</sub> + w<sub>L</sub> = 12 + 8 = 20 kN/m.
Global load factor γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.5 (given). Ultimate load w<sub>u</sub> = γ<sub>f</sub> w = 1.5 × 20 = 30 kN/m.
For a simply supported beam, M<sub>u,req</sub> = w<sub>u</sub> L² / 8, where L = 6.0 m.
examples.answer: The required ultimate moment is M<sub>u,req</sub> = 135 kNm.
examples.check:
span = 6.0
wD = 12.0
wL = 8.0
gf = 1.5
w_service = wD + wL
w_u = gf * w_service
Mu = w_u * span**2 / 8
print(w_service)
print(w_u)
print(Mu)

traps: Ultimate load and ultimate strength are not the same: the load acts on the member, while the strength resists it. The check compares a moment capacity with a moment demand.

Apply the global factor once to the service loads. The materials already enter at their ultimate values, f<sub>ck</sub> and f<sub>y</sub>, with no material factor. Do not add partial safety factors on top; that is limit state design, not the ultimate load method.
Do not mix this global load factor with the partial safety factors of Chapter 1.6. Numerically similar factors can mean different things.
ULM has no deflection or crack-width check. Passing M<sub>u</sub> ≥ M<sub>u,req</sub> does not prove serviceability.
Keep units consistent: w in kN/m with L in m gives M in kNm. The L² term is easy to forget.

quiz.a: A single number that multiplies the total service load to obtain the ultimate load; it covers all uncertainty together.

quiz.q: Why can a beam pass the ultimate load method and still be unsatisfactory in use?
quiz.a: ULM checks only collapse. Deflection and cracking at service loads are not checked, so service behaviour may still be poor.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam spans 5.0 m, with service dead load 10 kN/m and live load 6 kN/m. The global load factor is 1.5. Find the required ultimate moment.
quiz.a: Total service load = 16 kN/m; w<sub>u</sub> = 1.5 × 16 = 24 kN/m; M<sub>u,req</sub> = 24 × 5² / 8 = 75 kNm.

quiz.q: Why is one global factor less informative than separate partial factors?
quiz.a: It cannot distinguish dead-load variability from live-load variability, or concrete variability from steel variability. One factor hides which uncertainty dominates.

quiz.q: State the collapse check in the ultimate load method.
quiz.a: M<sub>u</sub> ≥ M<sub>u,req</sub>: the available ultimate moment must be at least the required ultimate moment.

quiz.q: Give the difference between ultimate load and ultimate strength.
quiz.a: Ultimate load is the factored load acting on the member. Ultimate strength is the capacity of the section to resist that load at collapse.

quiz.q: Which limitations of the ultimate load method led to limit state design?
quiz.a: It has no serviceability checks for deflection and cracking, and its single factor lumps load and material uncertainties. Limit state design adds serviceability checks and separate partial safety factors.

quiz.q: A section has M<sub>u</sub> = 150 kNm. With a global factor of 1.5, what maximum service moment can it resist?

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, collapse assessment now uses nonlinear section analysis, finite element models and load rating checks for bridges. Researchers test full-scale beams to compare predicted collapse moments with measured ones. Search for nonlinear analysis of reinforced concrete, load factor method history, and partial safety factors in IS 456.
